claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed primarily by grain-boundary-imposed kinetic barriers rather than configurational entropy alone.
Annealing-induced grain-boundary relaxation and controlled segregation reduce grain-boundary energy.
The initial material is a disordered nanocrystalline solid solution with minor secondary phases at grain boundaries.
Systematic annealing can manipulate grain-boundary characteristics while overall alloy composition remains constant.
Above 0.5 times the melting temperature, thermal activation enhances diffusion and makes grain-boundary-mediated processes significant.
Grain-boundary energy state, relaxation degree, and segregation profile are the relevant structural mediators.
Controlled annealing relaxes and modifies grain-boundary structure.
Lower grain-boundary energy increases the kinetic barrier to grain growth.
Annealing-modified grain boundaries increase the kinetic barrier to chemical segregation.
The enhanced grain-boundary barrier reduces structural coarsening at high temperature.
The enhanced grain-boundary barrier reduces high-temperature phase change.
The grain-boundary mechanism overshadows stabilization from configurational entropy.
Annealed samples with modified grain boundaries will exhibit slower grain growth than baseline samples.
Annealed samples with modified grain boundaries will exhibit less chemical inhomogeneity than baseline samples.
Slower grain growth and reduced chemical inhomogeneity constitute improved structural and chemical stability.
The prediction applies above 0.5 Tm and may not extend to lower temperatures or systems with negligible grain-boundary effects.
The magnitude of the stability effect depends on annealing parameters and intrinsic alloy composition.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis characterizes stabilization as primarily kinetic, but the stated effect of lowering grain-boundary energy is principally a reduction in the thermodynamic driving force for boundary migration; no explicit reason is given for treating that reduction as an increased kinetic barrier.

Controlled grain-boundary segregation is presented as a stabilizing modification, while reduced grain-boundary chemical inhomogeneity or segregation is also required as the favorable outcome. Beneficial controlled segregation is not distinguished from deleterious segregation, making the chemical prediction internally ambiguous.
